cards.text: Jerusalem has a problem, friend: the city is big and wide open, but there are few people in it, and the houses aren't rebuilt yet (Nehemiah 7:4). A whole city with NOBODY home? That's a cookie box with no cookies in it.

cards.question: Jerusalem needs people living inside those walls. Which group settles there?
The rest of the people take a vote to decide who else moves into Jerusalem.
Instead, the people cast lots. The lots pick ___ out of every ten people to live in Jerusalem.
After the lots are cast, the other nine out of every ten stay in their own towns.
Some men volunteer to live in Jerusalem. How do the people treat the men who volunteer?

cards.text: Then comes the roll call of who settles in Jerusalem: families from Judah and Benjamin, priests, Levites, and gatekeepers who keep watch at the gates. Every group gets a head count. Somebody was counting heads like it was their whole job, friend. Because it WAS.

Everyone else spreads out over the villages of Judah and Benjamin. Judah's people settle all the way from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom, and Benjamin's settle in towns like Michmash and Bethel. I spent YEARS in one drawer, and these folks get a whole map!

Next, the record goes back to the priests and Levites who went up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who led the first group home from exile (Ezra 2:1-2), and with Jeshua the high priest (Haggai 1:1). It traces the priestly families down through the generations, starting with Jeshua, the father of Joiakim. It ends with Levite leaders giving praise and thanksgiving as David the man of God prescribed, and gatekeepers guarding the storerooms at the gates.
They served in the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe. That's the roster, friend, but this city's story? NOT done.

findings.problem: The opening card tells only Nehemiah 7:4 and cites only that verse, which is outside the passage. It tells no part of Nehemiah 11:1-12:26 and does not set up 11:1. Outside facts are allowed when they help, but they should support a card that also tells part of the passage.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: "A whole city with NOBODY home?" stretches Nehemiah 7:4, which says there were few people in the city. The line works as a joke, but it states something the text shows is wrong, like the famine example.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes. ❌ "A famine. No food. NONE." ✅ "A famine. Food's running out." (Ruth 1:1)

findings.problem: Most choice cards in the stop come down to luck. Card 2 (which group settles), card 3 (vote or not, with nothing told about how they chose), and card 4 (one, three or five out of ten) give the baker nothing to reason from. Only card 5 is an informed follow-up, and card 6 is partly one. A few discovery questions are allowed, but here they are the majority. Card 3 in particular is a coin flip set up only to be corrected by card 4.

rule.text: A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: "Somebody was counting heads like it was their whole job, friend. Because it WAS." states as fact that someone in the passage had the job of counting. The text never says who counted or that it was anyone's job, so the storyteller line adds a fact.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can add a storyteller's line to carry the moment, like "But the Lord isn't finished with him," as long as it adds no facts.

findings.problem: Card 9 says Zerubbabel "led the first group home from exile (Ezra 2:1-2)." Ezra 2:1-2 lists those who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua and others, but it never calls this the first group or names Zerubbabel as its sole leader. Ezra 1:11 says Sheshbazzar brought the articles up when the exiles came up from Babylon.

rule.text: When he connects two passages, or explains what a law was for, he says only what the texts state.

findings.problem: Card 9 is a flat list summary with no trace of Papa Dorin's voice: no reaction, no comparison, no humor. It reads like a reference note rather than a storyteller.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Several summary cards for long stretches run past 2 sentences: card 7 has 4, and cards 8 and 9 have 3 each. prep-walkthrough.md says every story card after the opening is 1 to 2 sentences. But its own good genealogy example for a long stretch (Genesis 5) is 4 sentences, so the docs conflict.
findings.question: Can a summary story card for a long stretch go past the 1 to 2 sentence limit, as the Genesis 5 example does, or must it still be 1 to 2 sentences?
